records.source: וַיִּפְקֹ֣ד דָּוִ֔ד אֶת־הָעָ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתּ֑וֹ וַיָּ֣שֶׂם עֲלֵיהֶ֔ם שָׂרֵ֥י אֲלָפִ֖ים וְשָׂרֵ֥י מֵאֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And mustered David the people who [were] with him, and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.
pieces: David counted the troops who were with him and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds over them.

L.1: And David mustered the people who [were] with him, and he set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.

R.1: David gathered his soldiers and counted them. Then he chose commanders to lead them, some over units of a thousand men and some over units of a hundred.

decisions.choice: mustered: counted the men and organized them for battle
decisions.reason: The verb means to look over, count or call up. Here David reviews the men who had come to him at Mahanaim (17:24, 27) and puts them in order for the coming battle, as Saul did in 1 Samuel 11:8 and 15:4.

decisions.choice: commanders of thousands and of hundreds: officers over the army's larger and smaller units
decisions.reason: Israel's army was divided into units called thousands and hundreds, each with its own commander (Exodus 18:21; 1 Samuel 8:12; 22:7). The names are those of the units; a unit need not have held exactly that number of men.

decisions.choice: the people who were with him: the men who had fled with David and those who had joined him
decisions.reason: David had left Jerusalem with his household, his officials and his guard (15:16-18), and others had come to him since. Absalom now had the larger army of Israel (17:11, 24-26).

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); his soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: When "the people" means an army in the field, Literal keeps "the people", Balanced says "the troops" and Readable "the army" or "the soldiers".

decisions.choice: some over units of a thousand men and some over units of a hundred
decisions.reason: Readable spells out that thousands and hundreds are the sizes of the army's units.

records.heading: Absalom is defeated and killed

records.source: וַיְשַׁלַּ֨ח דָּוִ֜ד אֶת־הָעָ֗ם הַשְּׁלִשִׁ֤ית בְּיַד־יוֹאָב֙ וְ֠הַשְּׁלִשִׁית בְּיַ֨ד אֲבִישַׁ֤י בֶּן־צְרוּיָה֙ אֲחִ֣י יוֹאָ֔ב וְהַ֨שְּׁלִשִׁ֔ת בְּיַ֖ד אִתַּ֣י הַגִּתִּ֑יסוַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶל־הָעָ֔ם יָצֹ֥א אֵצֵ֛א גַּם־אֲנִ֖י עִמָּכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And sent out David the people, the third in [the] hand of Joab, and the third in [the] hand of Abishai son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab, and the third in [the] hand of Ittai the Gittite. And said the king to the people, Going out I will go out, also I, with you.
pieces: Then David sent the troops out in three divisions: one under Joab's command, one under Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one under Ittai the Gittite. The king told the troops, "I am going out with you myself."

L.2: And David sent out the people, a third under the hand of Joab, and a third under the hand of Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and a third under the hand of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the people, "I also will surely go out with you."

R.2: David sent the army out in three groups. Joab led one group. Joab's brother Abishai son of Zeruiah led another. Ittai from Gath led the third. The king told the soldiers, "I am going to march out with you too."

decisions.choice: in the hand of: under the command of
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power and control. A third of the army "in the hand of Joab" is the third he led.

decisions.choice: Ittai the Gittite: a man from the Philistine city of Gath who had joined David
decisions.reason: Ittai had come to David with six hundred men from Gath shortly before Absalom's revolt and had sworn to stay with him whatever happened (15:18-22). David now trusts this foreigner with a third of his army, next to his own nephews Joab and Abishai.

decisions.choice: I will surely go out, I also: a firm decision
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis, and "I also" stresses the king himself. David means to lead his men in person, as a king was expected to do (1 Samuel 8:20).

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); the army, the soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: When "the people" means an army in the field, Literal keeps "the people", Balanced says "the troops" and Readable "the army" or "the soldiers".

decisions.choice: Ittai from Gath
decisions.reason: Readable explains "the Gittite" as the man's home town.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הָעָ֜ם לֹ֣א תֵצֵ֗א כִּי֩ אִם־נֹ֨ס נָנ֜וּס לֹא־יָשִׂ֧ימוּ אֵלֵ֣ינוּ לֵ֗ב וְאִם־יָמֻ֤תוּ חֶצְיֵ֨נוּ֙ לֹֽא־יָשִׂ֤ימוּ אֵלֵ֨ינוּ֙ לֵ֔ב כִּֽי־עַתָּ֥ה כָמֹ֖נוּ עֲשָׂרָ֣ה אֲלָפִ֑ים וְעַתָּ֣ה ט֔וֹב כִּי־תִֽהְיֶה־לָּ֥נוּ מֵעִ֖יר לַעְזֽוֹר׃ס
records.gloss: And said the people, Not you shall go out, for if fleeing we flee, not they will set to us heart, and if die half of us, not they will set to us heart; for now like us [are] ten thousand; and now [it is] better that you be for us from [the] city to help.
pieces: But the troops said, "You must not go out. If we have to run, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth 10,000 of us. So it is better for you to help us from the city."

L.3: But the people said, "You shall not go out. For if we indeed flee, they will not set [their] heart on us; and if half of us die, they will not set [their] heart on us. For now [you are] like 10,000 of us. And now [it is] better that you be for us from the city to help."

R.3: But the soldiers said, "You must not go out to fight. If we have to run away, the enemy will not care about us. Even if half of us are killed, they will not care. You are the one they want. You are worth 10,000 of us! So it is better for you to stay in the city and be ready to help us from there."

decisions.choice: you are worth ten thousand of us
alternatives: for now there are ten thousand like us
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text as its vowels read it has "for now like us ten thousand". The Greek and Latin translations and a few Hebrew manuscripts read the same consonants as "you" instead of "now": "for you are like ten thousand of us". The Hebrew text can give the same sense if "you are" is understood, and the next words ("it is better that you ...") show that the soldiers are speaking about the king. Read the other way, the Hebrew would mean "there are ten thousand like us", that is, the rest of the army can be spared but the king cannot. Reviewers should check the manuscript evidence.

decisions.choice: they will not set their heart on us: the enemy will not care about us
decisions.reason: To set the heart on something is to pay attention to it. Absalom's men will not care how many of David's soldiers run or die, because their target is the king himself, as Ahithophel had advised (17:2).

decisions.choice: help us from the city: support the battle from Mahanaim
decisions.reason: The king would stay safe in the city and could send help or receive the army if it had to fall back.

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); the soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: When "the people" means an army in the field, Literal keeps "the people", Balanced says "the troops" and Readable "the army" or "the soldiers".

decisions.choice: the enemy; You are the one they want
decisions.reason: Readable names who "they" are and states what the soldiers imply: Absalom's men are after the king (17:2).

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶם֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־יִיטַ֥ב בְּעֵינֵיכֶ֖ם אֶעֱשֶׂ֑ה וַיַּעֲמֹ֤ד הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶל־יַ֣ד הַשַּׁ֔עַר וְכָל־הָעָם֙ יָֽצְא֔וּ לְמֵא֖וֹת וְלַאֲלָפִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said to them the king, What is good in your eyes I will do. And stood the king at [the] side of the gate, and all the people went out by hundreds and by thousands.
pieces: The king answered them, "I will do whatever you think best." So the king stood beside the gate while all the troops marched out in units of hundreds and of thousands.

L.4: And the king said to them, "Whatever is good in your eyes I will do." And the king stood beside the gate, and all the people went out by hundreds and by thousands.

R.4: The king told them, "I will do what you think is best." So he stood beside the city gate while the whole army marched out in groups of a hundred and of a thousand.

decisions.choice: good in your eyes: what you think best
decisions.reason: "In your eyes" means in your judgment. The king gives way to his men.

decisions.choice: the king stood beside the gate: watching his army march out
decisions.reason: The king took his place at the city gate as the units passed him, the last time he would see them before the battle. It is also where the men hear his order about Absalom (verse 5), and where he waits for news (verse 24).

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); the whole army (Readable)
decisions.reason: When "the people" means an army in the field, Literal keeps "the people", Balanced says "the troops" and Readable "the army" or "the soldiers".

records.source: וַיְצַ֣ו הַמֶּ֡לֶךְ אֶת־י֠וֹאָב וְאֶת־אֲבִישַׁ֤י וְאֶת־אִתַּי֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר לְאַט־לִ֖י לַנַּ֣עַר לְאַבְשָׁל֑וֹם וְכָל־הָעָ֣ם שָׁמְע֗וּ בְּצַוֺּ֥ת הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת־כָּל־הַשָּׂרִ֖ים עַל־דְּבַ֥ר אַבְשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: And commanded the king Joab and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Gently for me with the young man, with Absalom. And all the people heard when commanded the king all the commanders concerning [the] matter of Absalom.
pieces: The king gave an order to Joab, Abishai and Ittai: "For my sake, deal gently with the young man Absalom." All the troops heard the king give this order about Absalom to all the commanders.

L.5: And the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai, saying, "[Deal] gently for my sake with the young man, with Absalom." And all the people heard when the king commanded all the commanders concerning the matter of Absalom.

R.5: The king gave orders to Joab, Abishai and Ittai. He said, "For my sake, be gentle with young Absalom." All the soldiers heard the king give all the commanders this order about Absalom.

decisions.choice: gently for me: go easy on him, for my sake
decisions.reason: The phrase is short and urgent: "gently, for me". David asks his commanders to spare Absalom because of what Absalom means to him, not because Absalom deserves it.

decisions.choice: the young man: said with a father's affection
decisions.reason: The word can mean a boy, a young man or a servant. Absalom was a grown man with children (14:27) and was leading a revolt, but David speaks of him as "the young man", as if he were still a youth who could be forgiven. The word comes back in verses 12, 29 and 32.

decisions.choice: all the people heard: the whole army knew the order
decisions.reason: The narrator makes sure that no one could later claim not to know what the king wanted; the soldier in verse 12 says the same.

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); the soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: When "the people" means an army in the field, Literal keeps "the people", Balanced says "the troops" and Readable "the army" or "the soldiers".

records.source: וַיֵּצֵ֥א הָעָ֛ם הַשָּׂדֶ֖ה לִקְרַ֣את יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַתְּהִ֥י הַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה בְּיַ֥עַר אֶפְרָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And went out the people [to] the field to meet Israel, and was the battle in [the] forest of Ephraim.
pieces: The army marched out into the open country to face Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.

L.6: And the people went out into the field to meet Israel, and the battle was in the forest of Ephraim.

R.6: So David's army went out into the countryside to fight the army of Israel. The battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.

decisions.choice: Israel: the Israelites who had followed Absalom
decisions.reason: "Israel" here is Absalom's army, drawn from the tribes who had turned to him (15:13; 17:11, 24-26), set against David's own men.

decisions.choice: the forest of Ephraim: a wooded region east of the Jordan
decisions.reason: The battle was fought near Mahanaim in Gilead (17:24, 26), east of the Jordan, not in the tribal land of Ephraim west of the river. Why the woods there carried Ephraim's name is not known.

decisions.choice: to meet: to meet in battle
decisions.reason: The verb "meet" often means going out against an enemy (1 Samuel 4:1; 17:48).

decisions.choice: the army (Balanced); David's army (Readable)
decisions.reason: When "the people" means an army in the field, Literal keeps "the people", Balanced says "the troops" and Readable "the army" or "the soldiers". Readable names David to make clear which army is meant.

records.source: וַיִּנָּ֤גְפוּ שָׁם֙ עַ֣ם יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לִפְנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֣י דָוִ֑ד וַתְּהִי־שָׁ֞ם הַמַּגֵּפָ֧ה גְדוֹלָ֛ה בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא עֶשְׂרִ֥ים אָֽלֶף׃
records.gloss: And were defeated there [the] people of Israel before [the] servants of David, and was there the slaughter great on that day, twenty thousand.
pieces: There the army of Israel was defeated by David's men, and the slaughter there that day was great: 20,000 men.

L.7: And the people of Israel were struck down there before the servants of David, and the slaughter there was great on that day: 20,000.

R.7: David's men beat the army of Israel there. Many men were killed that day: 20,000 of them.

decisions.choice: the servants of David: the soldiers loyal to David
decisions.reason: "Servants" here are the men who serve the king as soldiers, as in 2:12-17.

decisions.choice: were struck down; the slaughter: a heavy defeat with many dead
decisions.reason: The verb and the noun come from the same root, "strike". Israel was not only beaten but suffered great losses.

decisions.choice: David's men
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "servants"; Balanced and Readable say "men", since these are David's soldiers, not household servants.
The Hebrew gives only the number; Balanced and Readable add "men".

records.source: וַתְּהִי־שָׁ֧ם הַמִּלְחָמָ֛ה נָפֹ֖צֶתעַל־פְּנֵ֣י כָל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיֶּ֤רֶב הַיַּ֨עַר֙ לֶאֱכֹ֣ל בָּעָ֔ם מֵאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָכְלָ֛ה הַחֶ֖רֶב בַּיּ֥וֹם הַהֽוּא׃
records.gloss: And was there the battle spread over [the] face of all the land, and more [did] the forest to devour among the people than what devoured the sword on that day.
pieces: The fighting spread out over the whole countryside, and the forest claimed more lives that day than the sword did.

L.8: And the battle there was spread over the face of all the land, and the forest devoured more among the people than the sword devoured on that day.

R.8: The fighting spread all over the countryside. That day the forest killed more men than the swords did.

decisions.choice: the forest devoured more than the sword: more died in the forest than in the fighting
decisions.reason: Swords "devour" in Hebrew idiom (2:26; 11:25). Here the forest itself is said to devour: men fleeing through thick woods, rough ground and pits died there in greater numbers than in combat. The text does not say how; Absalom's own end (verses 9 and 17) shows the forest at work.

decisions.choice: all the land: the whole area of the battle
decisions.reason: The word can mean a country or a stretch of ground. Here it is the region around the forest, not all Israel.

decisions.choice: claimed more lives
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of the forest as a killer without the word "devour".

records.source: וַיִּקָּרֵא֙ אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם לִפְנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֣י דָוִ֑ד וְאַבְשָׁל֞וֹם רֹכֵ֣ב עַל־הַפֶּ֗רֶד וַיָּבֹ֣א הַפֶּ֡רֶד תַּ֣חַת שׂוֹבֶךְ֩ הָאֵלָ֨ה הַגְּדוֹלָ֜ה וַיֶּחֱזַ֧ק רֹאשׁ֣וֹ בָאֵלָ֗ה וַיֻּתַּן֙ בֵּ֤ין הַשָּׁמַ֨יִם֙ וּבֵ֣ין הָאָ֔רֶץ וְהַפֶּ֥רֶד אֲשֶׁר־תַּחְתָּ֖יו עָבָֽר׃
records.gloss: And happened to meet Absalom before [the] servants of David, and Absalom [was] riding on the mule, and went the mule under [the] thick branches of the terebinth, the great [one], and held fast his head in the terebinth, and he was put between the heavens and between the earth, and the mule that [was] under him passed on.
pieces: Absalom happened to come upon some of David's men. He was riding his mule, and when it passed beneath the tangled branches of a great terebinth, Absalom's head was caught fast in the tree. He was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him kept going.

L.9: And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. And Absalom [was] riding on the mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of the great terebinth, and his head caught fast in the terebinth, and he was left between the heavens and the earth, and the mule that [was] under him passed on.

R.9: Absalom happened to run into some of David's men. He was riding on his mule. The mule went under the thick branches of a big tree, and Absalom's head got stuck in the branches. He was left hanging in the air, and the mule ran on without him.

decisions.choice: happened to meet: came upon them by chance
decisions.reason: The verb form describes an encounter that was not planned. Absalom, fleeing or riding through the forest, suddenly finds himself in front of David's soldiers.

decisions.choice: the mule: the mount of the king's sons
decisions.reason: Mules were ridden by David's sons (13:29), and David has Solomon ride his own mule at his crowning (1 Kings 1:33). Absalom rides as a prince, and the mule going on without him is a picture of his kingship leaving him.

decisions.choice: his head caught fast: his head was wedged in the branches
alternatives: his hair caught in the tree
decisions.reason: The text says that his head was caught. Absalom's thick hair has been mentioned (14:26), and many readers have pictured him caught by it, but this verse does not say so.

decisions.choice: between the heavens and the earth: hanging in midair
decisions.reason: The phrase describes something hanging above the ground with nothing below it (compare 1 Chronicles 21:16). Absalom hangs helpless, neither riding nor standing.

decisions.choice: the terebinth: a large, spreading tree
decisions.reason: The word names a big tree, the terebinth or a kind of oak, as in Judges 6:11.

decisions.choice: a big tree; hanging in the air
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for the terebinth and for "between the heavens and the earth".

decisions.choice: David's men
decisions.reason: As in verse 7.

records.source: וַיַּרְא֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶחָ֔ד וַיַּגֵּ֖ד לְיוֹאָ֑ב וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הִנֵּה֙ רָאִ֣יתִי אֶת־אַבְשָׁלֹ֔ם תָּל֖וּי בָּאֵלָֽה׃
records.gloss: And saw a man, one, and told Joab, and said, Look, I saw Absalom hanging in the terebinth.
pieces: One man saw it and told Joab, "I have just seen Absalom hanging in a terebinth!"

L.10: And a certain man saw [it] and told Joab, and he said, "Look, I saw Absalom hanging in the terebinth."

R.10: One of the soldiers saw this and told Joab, "I saw Absalom hanging in a tree!"

decisions.choice: look: a word that calls attention to surprising news
decisions.reason: The man stresses what he has seen: the king's son, hanging helpless in a tree.

decisions.choice: One of the soldiers
decisions.reason: Readable says that the man was one of David's soldiers, as verses 9 and 12 make clear.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב לָאִישׁ֙ הַמַּגִּ֣יד ל֔וֹ וְהִנֵּ֣ה רָאִ֔יתָ וּמַדּ֛וּעַ לֹֽא־הִכִּית֥וֹ שָׁ֖ם אָ֑רְצָה וְעָלַ֗י לָ֤תֶת לְךָ֙ עֲשָׂ֣רָה כֶ֔סֶף וַחֲגֹרָ֖ה אֶחָֽת׃
records.gloss: And said Joab to the man who told him, And look, you saw, and why not did you strike him there to the ground? And on me [it would have been] to give to you ten [of] silver and one belt.
pieces: Joab said to the man who had told him, "You saw him? Then why did you not strike him down to the ground right there? I would have given you {{units:about 4 ounces of silver|ten shekels of silver}} and a belt."

L.11: And Joab said to the man who told him, "And look, you saw [him]! Then why did you not strike him there to the ground? And it would have been on me to give you ten [shekels of] silver and a belt."

R.11: Joab said to the man, "You saw him? Then why did you not kill him right there and let him fall to the ground? I would have given you {{units:about 4 ounces of silver|ten shekels of silver}} and a soldier's belt."

decisions.choice: strike him to the ground: kill him
decisions.reason: To strike someone down "to the ground" is to kill him. Joab does not hide that he wanted Absalom dead, in spite of the king's order (verse 5).

decisions.choice: ten of silver: ten shekels of silver
decisions.reason: The unit is not named, but sums of silver were normally weighed in shekels. Ten shekels was a good reward for a soldier.

decisions.choice: a belt: a warrior's belt, given as an honor
decisions.reason: A belt held a soldier's sword and was a sign of rank; Jonathan gave David his belt with his armor (1 Samuel 18:4). Joab offers both money and honor.

decisions.choice: on me to give: it would have been my part to give
decisions.reason: Joab means that he would gladly have paid the reward himself.

decisions.choice: about 4 ounces of silver
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the weight in modern terms, with the shekel as the alternative; Literal supplies the unit in brackets.

decisions.choice: kill him ... and let him fall to the ground; a soldier's belt
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what "strike him to the ground" means and what kind of belt it was.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָאִישׁ֙ אֶל־יוֹאָ֔ב וְל֨וּאאָנֹכִ֜י שֹׁקֵ֤ל עַל־כַּפַּי֙ אֶ֣לֶף כֶּ֔סֶף לֹֽא־אֶשְׁלַ֥ח יָדִ֖י אֶל־בֶּן־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ כִּ֣י בְאָזְנֵ֜ינוּ צִוָּ֣ה הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ אֹ֠תְךָ וְאֶת־אֲבִישַׁ֤י וְאֶת־אִתַּי֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר שִׁמְרוּ־מִ֕י בַּנַּ֖עַר בְּאַבְשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: And said the man to Joab, And if I [were] weighing on my palms a thousand [of] silver, not would I stretch out my hand against [the] son of the king; for in our ears commanded the king you and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Guard, whoever, the young man, Absalom.
pieces: But the man answered Joab, "Even if I felt the weight of {{units:about 25 pounds of silver|a thousand shekels of silver}} in my hands, I would not raise my hand against the king's son. We all heard the king command you and Abishai and Ittai, 'Whoever you are, keep the young man Absalom safe.'

L.12: And the man said to Joab, "Even if I were weighing 1,000 [shekels of] silver on my palms, I would not stretch out my hand against the king's son. For in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, saying, 'Guard, whoever [you are], the young man Absalom.'

R.12: But the man answered Joab, "Even if someone put {{units:about 25 pounds of silver|a thousand shekels of silver}} in my hands, I would not hurt the king's son. We all heard the king give this order to you and Abishai and Ittai: 'Whoever you are, keep young Absalom safe.'

decisions.choice: even if: the reading the scribes marked
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "and not"; the reading the scribes marked to be read aloud (qere) is "and if", which gives the sense "even if". The marked reading fits the sentence and is followed.

decisions.choice: weighing a thousand on my palms: even if the money were paid out into my hands
decisions.reason: Silver was paid by weighing it. The man answers Joab's offer of ten shekels (verse 11): not even a hundred times as much would make him do it.

decisions.choice: stretch out my hand against: attack, harm
decisions.reason: The same phrase is used of not harming the Lord's anointed (1 Samuel 24:7; 26:9). The man treats the king's son with the same caution.

decisions.choice: guard, whoever you are, the young man: let every one of you protect him
alternatives: guard the young man for me
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "whoever" is unusual here: the king's order covered anyone who met Absalom. A few Hebrew manuscripts and some early translations read "for me" instead ("guard the young man for me"), as in verse 5. The Hebrew text is followed.

decisions.choice: about 25 pounds of silver
decisions.reason: A thousand shekels is about 25 pounds. Balanced and Readable give the modern weight, with the shekel as the alternative.

decisions.choice: We all heard
decisions.reason: "In our ears" means that the soldiers heard it themselves (verse 5).

records.source: אֽוֹ־עָשִׂ֤יתִי בְנַפְשִׁי֙ שֶׁ֔קֶר וְכָל־דָּבָ֖ר לֹא־יִכָּחֵ֣ד מִן־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְאַתָּ֖ה תִּתְיַצֵּ֥ב מִנֶּֽגֶד׃
records.gloss: Or I had done against my life falsehood, and any thing not is hidden from the king, and you, you would stand from in front.
pieces: And if I had acted treacherously and put my own life at risk, you yourself would have stood back and kept out of it, because nothing is hidden from the king."

L.13: Or [if] I had dealt falsely against my own life, and nothing is hidden from the king, then you yourself would have stood aloof."

R.13: If I had disobeyed the king and killed Absalom, I would have lost my own life. The king finds out everything. And you would not have stood up for me."

decisions.choice: against my own life: the reading the scribes marked
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "and my life"; the reading marked to be read aloud (qere) is "against my life", that is, at the cost of my own life. Some read the phrase as "against his life", meaning Absalom's, but that needs a change to the text. Either way the man means that killing Absalom would have been a betrayal of the king that he would have paid for himself.

decisions.choice: falsehood: an act of treachery against the king's order
decisions.reason: The word means lying or deceit. To kill Absalom after the king's public order would be to act falsely toward the king.

decisions.choice: nothing is hidden from the king: the king would find out
decisions.reason: The woman of Tekoa said the same of David's wisdom (14:20). The soldier knows that he could not hide what he had done.

decisions.choice: you would stand aloof: you would not take my side
decisions.reason: To stand "at a distance" is to keep apart from someone in trouble. The soldier expects that Joab would have left him to face the king alone.

decisions.choice: because nothing is hidden from the king
decisions.reason: Balanced moves the remark to the end, where it reads as the reason the soldier would have been found out.

decisions.choice: disobeyed the king and killed Absalom; I would have lost my own life
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the treachery would have been and what "against my life" means.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֔ב לֹא־כֵ֖ן אֹחִ֣ילָה לְפָנֶ֑יךָ וַיִּקַּח֩ שְׁלֹשָׁ֨ה שְׁבָטִ֜ים בְּכַפּ֗וֹ וַיִּתְקָעֵם֙ בְּלֵ֣ב אַבְשָׁל֔וֹם עוֹדֶ֥נּוּ חַ֖י בְּלֵ֥ב הָאֵלָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said Joab, Not thus will I wait before you. And he took three rods in his palm and thrust them into [the] heart of Absalom, still he [was] alive in [the] heart of the terebinth.
pieces: Joab said, "I will not waste any more time with you like this." He took three rods in his hand and drove them into Absalom's chest while Absalom was still alive in the middle of the tree.

L.14: And Joab said, "Not so will I wait before you." And he took three rods in his palm and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he [was] still alive in the heart of the terebinth.

R.14: Joab said, "I am not going to stand here waiting for you." He took three sticks in his hand and drove them into Absalom's chest. Absalom was still alive, hanging in the tree.

decisions.choice: rods: sticks or clubs, perhaps pointed
decisions.reason: The word usually means a rod, staff or club. The ancient Greek translation reads "darts". Joab's blows do not kill Absalom at once; his armor-bearers finish him (verse 15).

decisions.choice: the heart of Absalom ... the heart of the terebinth: his chest, in the middle of the tree
decisions.reason: "Heart" is used twice: of Absalom's body and of the middle of the tree. The repeated word ties the man and the tree together.

decisions.choice: not so will I wait before you: I will not stand here arguing
decisions.reason: Joab cuts the conversation short and acts himself.

decisions.choice: Absalom's chest
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "chest" for the first "heart", since Absalom was not killed at once; Literal keeps the repeated word.

decisions.choice: sticks
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday word for rods.

records.source: וַיָּסֹ֨בּוּ֙ עֲשָׂרָ֣ה נְעָרִ֔ים נֹשְׂאֵ֖י כְּלֵ֣י יוֹאָ֑ב וַיַּכּ֥וּ אֶת־אַבְשָׁל֖וֹם וַיְמִיתֻֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And surrounded ten young men, bearers of [the] weapons of Joab, and struck Absalom and killed him.
pieces: Then ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, closed in around Absalom, struck him down and killed him.

L.15: And ten young men, bearers of Joab's weapons, surrounded [him] and struck Absalom and killed him.

R.15: Then ten young men who carried Joab's weapons for him gathered around Absalom. They attacked him and killed him.

decisions.choice: bearers of Joab's weapons: his armor-bearers
decisions.reason: An armor-bearer carried a warrior's weapons and fought at his side (1 Samuel 14:6-14; 31:4-5). Ten of them show Joab's high rank.

decisions.choice: struck and killed him: they finished him off
decisions.reason: Joab wounded Absalom; his men gave the blows that killed him.

decisions.choice: Joab's armor-bearers
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "bearers of the weapons" is the usual English "armor-bearers"; Literal keeps the longer phrase.

records.source: וַיִּתְקַ֤ע יוֹאָב֙ בַּשֹּׁפָ֔ר וַיָּ֣שָׁב הָעָ֔ם מִרְדֹ֖ף אַחֲרֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּֽי־חָשַׂ֥ךְ יוֹאָ֖ב אֶת־הָעָֽם׃
records.gloss: And blew Joab on the trumpet, and turned back the people from pursuing after Israel, for held back Joab the people.
pieces: Then Joab sounded the trumpet, and the troops turned back from chasing Israel, because Joab held the army back.

L.16: And Joab blew the trumpet, and the people turned back from pursuing after Israel, for Joab held back the people.

R.16: Then Joab blew the ram's horn, and his soldiers stopped chasing the men of Israel. Joab held them back.

decisions.choice: trumpet: a ram's horn, blown as a signal in war
decisions.reason: As in 2:28, the shofar tells the army to stop fighting.

decisions.choice: for Joab held back the people: he stopped the killing
decisions.reason: With Absalom dead the revolt was over, and the men fleeing were David's own people. The text does not give Joab's reason, but compare 2:26-28, where Joab also stops a pursuit of fellow Israelites.

decisions.choice: the troops, the army (Balanced); his soldiers (Readable)
decisions.reason: When "the people" means an army in the field, Literal keeps "the people", Balanced says "the troops" and Readable "the army" or "the soldiers".

decisions.choice: the ram's horn
decisions.reason: Readable names the instrument itself, as in 2:28.

records.source: וַיִּקְח֣וּ אֶת־אַבְשָׁל֗וֹם וַיַּשְׁלִ֨יכוּ אֹת֤וֹ בַיַּ֨עַר֙ אֶל־הַפַּ֣חַת הַגָּד֔וֹל וַיַּצִּ֧בוּ עָלָ֛יו גַּל־אֲבָנִ֖ים גָּד֣וֹל מְאֹ֑ד וְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל נָ֖סוּ אִ֥ישׁ לְאֹהָלָֽיו׃ס
records.gloss: And they took Absalom and threw him in the forest into the pit, the great [one], and set up over him a heap of stones very great; and all Israel fled, each to his tents.
pieces: They took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest, then raised a huge heap of stones over him. And all Israel fled, every man to his home.

L.17: And they took Absalom and threw him into the great pit in the forest, and they set up over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled, each to his tent.

R.17: They took Absalom's body and threw it into a big hole in the forest. Then they piled a huge heap of stones on top of it. All the men of Israel ran away to their homes.

decisions.choice: a heap of stones over him: the burial of a man under a curse
decisions.reason: A heap of stones was raised over Achan and over the king of Ai (Joshua 7:26; 8:29). Absalom gets no family tomb, only a pit in the forest; the next verse sets this beside the pillar he had built for himself.

decisions.choice: each to his tent: each man to his home
decisions.reason: "To your tents" is an old way of saying "go home" (20:1; 1 Kings 12:16). Absalom's army broke up and went home.

decisions.choice: his tent: written and marked readings agree in sense
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "his tent"; the reading marked to be read aloud (qere) is "his tents". The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: every man to his home (Balanced); to their homes (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom.

decisions.choice: Absalom's body
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that Absalom was already dead.

records.source: וְאַבְשָׁלֹ֣ם לָקַ֗ח וַיַּצֶּב־ל֤וֹ בְחַיָּיו֙ אֶת־מַצֶּ֨בֶת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּעֵֽמֶק־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּ֤י אָמַר֙ אֵֽין־לִ֣י בֵ֔ן בַּעֲב֖וּר הַזְכִּ֣יר שְׁמִ֑י וַיִּקְרָ֤א לַמַּצֶּ֨בֶת֙ עַל־שְׁמ֔וֹ וַיִּקָּ֤רֵא לָהּ֙ יַ֣ד אַבְשָׁלֹ֔ם עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And Absalom had taken and set up for himself in his life the pillar which [is] in [the] Valley of the King, for he said, There is not to me a son in order to cause to remember my name; and he called the pillar by his name, and it is called Monument of Absalom until this day.
pieces: During his lifetime Absalom had taken a pillar and set it up for himself in the King's Valley, because he said, "I have no son to keep my name remembered." He named the pillar after himself, and it is called Absalom's Monument to this day.

L.18: Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar that [is] in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name remembered." And he called the pillar by his own name, and it is called Absalom's Monument to this day.

R.18: While Absalom was still alive, he had set up a stone pillar for himself in the King's Valley. He said, "I have no son to keep people remembering my name." So he named the pillar after himself. It is called Absalom's Monument to this day.

decisions.choice: I have no son: at the time he set up the pillar, Absalom had no living son
alternatives: the pillar was set up before his sons were born
the two notices come from different reports
decisions.reason: In 14:27 Absalom had three sons and a daughter named Tamar. The two notices can fit if the sons died young (the sons are not named, while the daughter is), or if the pillar was set up before they were born. They may also come from different reports that the writer placed side by side. The text does not explain it.

decisions.choice: had taken and set up: an earlier act told here as an aside
decisions.reason: The verse breaks off the story to tell what Absalom had done before. Its place, right after the heap of stones over his body (verse 17), sets his proud monument beside his shameful grave.

decisions.choice: the pillar in the King's Valley: a memorial stone near Jerusalem
decisions.reason: A standing stone could mark a grave or keep a name alive (Genesis 35:20). The King's Valley is named in Genesis 14:17 as another name for the Valley of Shaveh, near Salem, which was taken to be Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: monument: literally "hand"
decisions.reason: The word "hand" is used for a memorial, as in 1 Samuel 15:12, where Saul set up a monument for himself.

decisions.choice: to this day: the writer's own day
decisions.reason: As in 4:3 and 6:8, the pillar was still known by that name when the account was written.

decisions.choice: a stone pillar
decisions.reason: Readable says what the pillar was made of.

records.source: וַאֲחִימַ֤עַץ בֶּן־צָדוֹק֙ אָמַ֔ר אָר֣וּצָה נָּ֔א וַאֲבַשְּׂרָ֖ה אֶת־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ כִּי־שְׁפָט֥וֹ יְהוָ֖ה מִיַּ֥ד אֹיְבָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, Let me run, please, and bring news [to] the king, that has judged him Yahweh from [the] hand of his enemies.
pieces: Then Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Let me run and take the news to the king that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has vindicated him by rescuing him from his enemies."

L.19: And Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Please let me run and bring news [to] the king, that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has vindicated him from the hand of his enemies."

R.19: Ahimaaz son of Zadok said to Joab, "Please let me run to the king with the good news. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has rescued him from his enemies and shown that he was in the right."

decisions.choice: Ahimaaz son of Zadok: the priest's son who had already carried news to David
decisions.reason: Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar had brought David word of Absalom's plans at the risk of their lives (15:27, 36; 17:17-21). He is a swift and trusted runner.

decisions.choice: bring news: as a rule, good news
decisions.reason: The verb is used for bringing news, most often good news of victory (1 Samuel 31:9; 2 Samuel 4:10). Ahimaaz thinks of the victory; Joab thinks of how David will take Absalom's death (verse 20).

decisions.choice: judged him from the hand of his enemies: gave him justice by setting him free from them
decisions.reason: To "judge someone from the hand" of an enemy is to decide his case in his favor and so rescue him (1 Samuel 24:16). Yahweh has shown that David was in the right against the rebels. The Cushite uses the same words in verse 31.

decisions.choice: vindicated
decisions.reason: "Judged" alone would sound like a sentence against David. Literal and Balanced say "vindicated", and Balanced adds "by rescuing him" for "from the hand of".

decisions.choice: said to Joab; the good news
decisions.reason: Readable names Joab, to whom Ahimaaz is speaking (verse 20), and says that the news is good.

records.heading: David hears the news

records.source: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ יוֹאָ֗ב לֹא֩ אִ֨ישׁ בְּשֹׂרָ֤ה אַתָּה֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה וּבִשַּׂרְתָּ֖ בְּי֣וֹם אַחֵ֑ר וְהַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ לֹ֣א תְבַשֵּׂ֔ר כִּֽי־עַל־כֵּ֥ןבֶּן־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מֵֽת׃
records.gloss: And said to him Joab, Not a man of news [are] you this day, and you will bring news on another day; and this day not will you bring news, because therefore the son of the king [is] dead.
pieces: But Joab told him, "You are not the one to carry the news today. You may carry news another day, but not today, because the king's son is dead."

L.20: And Joab said to him, "You [are] not a man of news this day. You may bring news on another day, but this day you shall not bring news, because the king's son is dead."

R.20: But Joab told him, "You are not the right man to take the news today. You can take news some other day, but not today. The king's son is dead."

decisions.choice: not a man of news today: Joab keeps Ahimaaz from carrying news of Absalom's death
decisions.reason: News of the death of the king's son would not be good news to David. A messenger who brought such news could be blamed or worse, as the man who brought word of Saul's death was (1:15; 4:10). Joab may be protecting Ahimaaz, and perhaps also himself.

decisions.choice: because: one word is written but not read
decisions.reason: After "because" the Hebrew text writes "therefore", but the scribes marked one of its two words as not to be read aloud. Read as marked, the clause simply gives the reason: the king's son is dead.

decisions.choice: The king's son is dead.
decisions.reason: Readable states the reason as a sentence of its own.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יוֹאָב֙ לַכּוּשִׁ֔י לֵ֛ךְ הַגֵּ֥ד לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֣ר רָאִ֑יתָה וַיִּשְׁתַּ֧חוּ כוּשִׁ֛י לְיוֹאָ֖ב וַיָּרֹֽץ׃
records.gloss: And said Joab to the Cushite, Go, tell the king what you have seen. And bowed [the] Cushite to Joab and ran.
pieces: Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go and tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed down to Joab and ran off.

L.21: And Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." And the Cushite bowed down to Joab and ran.

R.21: Then Joab told a man from Cush, "Go and tell the king what you saw." The man bowed down to Joab and ran off.

decisions.choice: the Cushite: a man from Cush, south of Egypt
decisions.reason: Cush was the land along the upper Nile, south of Egypt. The man was a foreigner, perhaps a servant or a soldier in Joab's army. The word is used as his description, not as his name.

decisions.choice: bowed down to Joab: took his orders with respect
decisions.reason: The Cushite bows to his commander before he sets out, unlike Ahimaaz, who argues with Joab (verses 22-23).

decisions.choice: a man from Cush; the man
decisions.reason: Readable explains "Cushite" as the man's homeland.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨סֶף ע֜וֹד אֲחִימַ֤עַץ בֶּן־צָדוֹק֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל־יוֹאָ֔ב וִ֣יהִי מָ֔ה אָרֻֽצָה־נָּ֥א גַם־אָ֖נִי אַחֲרֵ֣י הַכּוּשִׁ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב לָֽמָּה־זֶּ֞ה אַתָּ֥ה רָץ֙ בְּנִ֔י וּלְכָ֖ה אֵין־בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה מֹצֵֽאת׃
records.gloss: And added again Ahimaaz son of Zadok and said to Joab, And let be whatever, let me run, please, also I, after the Cushite. And said Joab, Why this [are] you running, my son, and for you there is no news finding?
pieces: Ahimaaz son of Zadok spoke to Joab again. "Whatever happens," he said, "please let me run after the Cushite too." Joab replied, "Why would you want to run, my son? You have no news that will bring you any reward."

L.22: And Ahimaaz son of Zadok spoke again and said to Joab, "Whatever may happen, please let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why [is] this, [that] you would run, my son, when for you there is no news that will find [a reward]?"

R.22: But Ahimaaz son of Zadok asked Joab again, "No matter what happens, please let me run after the Cushite too." Joab answered, "My son, why do you want to run? You will get no reward for this news."

decisions.choice: let be whatever: come what may
decisions.reason: Ahimaaz accepts whatever may follow. He repeats the words in verse 23.

decisions.choice: news that finds: news that will earn a reward
alternatives: you have no news that will reach the king in time
decisions.reason: The word for news can also mean the reward given to a messenger for good news (4:10). Joab tells Ahimaaz that this news will bring him nothing, or nothing good.

decisions.choice: my son: a friendly address from an older man
decisions.reason: Joab is not Ahimaaz's father. He speaks kindly to the younger man.

decisions.choice: any reward; no reward
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the short Hebrew phrase.

records.source: וִיהִי־מָ֣ה אָר֔וּץ וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֖וֹ ר֑וּץ וַיָּ֤רָץ אֲחִימַ֨עַץ֙ דֶּ֣רֶךְ הַכִּכָּ֔ר וַֽיַּעֲבֹ֖ר אֶת־הַכּוּשִֽׁי׃
records.gloss: And let be whatever, I will run. And he said to him, Run. And ran Ahimaaz [by the] way of the plain and passed the Cushite.
pieces: "Whatever happens," Ahimaaz said, "I want to run." "Then run," Joab told him. So Ahimaaz ran by the road through the plain and got ahead of the Cushite.

L.23: "And whatever may happen, I will run." And he said to him, "Run." And Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and he passed the Cushite.

R.23: Ahimaaz said, "No matter what happens, I am going to run." So Joab told him, "Run!" Ahimaaz took the road through the Jordan Valley and passed the Cushite.

decisions.choice: the way of the plain: the road through the floor of the Jordan Valley
decisions.reason: The word means a round, flat area, and is used of the Jordan plain (Genesis 13:10-12). Ahimaaz seems to have taken a longer but easier route along the valley, while the Cushite went straight across the hills, and so Ahimaaz arrived first. The text does not describe the Cushite's route.

decisions.choice: whatever may happen, I will run: Ahimaaz insists
decisions.reason: Ahimaaz's words follow Joab's question in verse 22 without a new "he said". His insistence wins Joab's permission.

decisions.choice: Ahimaaz said; Joab told him
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not repeat the speakers' names; Balanced and Readable add them to make clear who speaks.

decisions.choice: the Jordan Valley
decisions.reason: Readable names the plain.

records.source: וְדָוִ֥ד יוֹשֵׁ֖ב בֵּין־שְׁנֵ֣י הַשְּׁעָרִ֑ים וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ הַצֹּפֶ֜ה אֶל־גַּ֤ג הַשַּׁ֨עַר֙ אֶל־הַ֣חוֹמָ֔ה וַיִּשָּׂ֤א אֶת־עֵינָיו֙ וַיַּ֔רְא וְהִנֵּה־אִ֖ישׁ רָ֥ץ לְבַדּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And David [was] sitting between [the] two gates; and went the watchman to [the] roof of the gate, to the wall, and lifted up his eyes and saw, and look, a man running alone.
pieces: David was sitting between the inner and outer gates. The watchman went up to the roof over the gate, on the wall. He looked out and saw a man running alone.

L.24: And David [was] sitting between the two gates. And the watchman went to the roof of the gate by the wall, and he lifted up his eyes and looked, and there [was] a man running alone.

R.24: David was sitting in the gateway, between the city's inner and outer gates. The watchman went up on the roof over the gateway, on top of the city wall. He looked out and saw a man running by himself.

decisions.choice: between the two gates: inside the gateway
decisions.reason: A walled city's gateway often had an outer and an inner gate with a space between them. David waits there, where news would arrive first (verse 4).

decisions.choice: lifted up his eyes and saw: looked into the distance
decisions.reason: The phrase describes looking up and seeing something, as in Genesis 18:2.

decisions.choice: the inner and outer gates
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the two gates were.

records.source: וַיִּקְרָ֤א הַצֹּפֶה֙ וַיַּגֵּ֣ד לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אִם־לְבַדּ֖וֹ בְּשׂוֹרָ֣ה בְּפִ֑יו וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ הָל֖וֹךְ וְקָרֵֽב׃
records.gloss: And called out the watchman and told the king. And said the king, If [he is] alone, news [is] in his mouth. And he came, coming and drawing near.
pieces: The watchman called down and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he is bringing news." The man came closer and closer.

L.25: And the watchman called out and told the king. And the king said, "If he [is] alone, news [is] in his mouth." And he kept coming and drawing near.

R.25: The watchman shouted down and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he must have news." The runner kept coming closer and closer.

decisions.choice: if he is alone, he has news: a single runner is a messenger
decisions.reason: Men fleeing a lost battle would come in groups; one man running alone was likely a messenger sent with a report.

decisions.choice: he came, coming and drawing near: he came steadily closer
decisions.reason: The repeated verb describes continuing movement.

decisions.choice: he is bringing news; he must have news
decisions.reason: "News in his mouth" is put plainly.

records.source: וַיַּ֣רְא הַצֹּפֶה֮ אִישׁ־אַחֵ֣ר רָץ֒ וַיִּקְרָ֤א הַצֹּפֶה֙ אֶל־הַשֹּׁעֵ֔ר וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּה־אִ֖ישׁ רָ֣ץ לְבַדּ֑וֹ וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ גַּם־זֶ֥ה מְבַשֵּֽׂר׃
records.gloss: And saw the watchman another man running, and called the watchman to the gatekeeper and said, Look, a man running alone. And said the king, Also this [one is] bringing news.
pieces: Then the watchman saw another man running, and he called down to the gatekeeper, "Look, there is a man running alone!" The king said, "He is bringing news too."

L.26: And the watchman saw another man running, and the watchman called to the gatekeeper and said, "Look, a man running alone!" And the king said, "This one also [is] bringing news."

R.26: Then the watchman saw a second man running. He shouted to the gatekeeper, "Look! There is another man running by himself!" The king said, "He must be bringing news too."

decisions.choice: the gatekeeper: the man in charge of the gate
decisions.reason: The watchman on the roof calls to the gatekeeper below, who passes the word to the king sitting in the gateway.

decisions.choice: another man
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that this is the second runner.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַצֹּפֶ֔ה אֲנִ֤י רֹאֶה֙ אֶת־מְרוּצַ֣ת הָרִאשׁ֔וֹן כִּמְרֻצַ֖ת אֲחִימַ֣עַץ בֶּן־צָד֑וֹק וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אִֽישׁ־ט֣וֹב זֶ֔ה וְאֶל־בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה טוֹבָ֖ה יָבֽוֹא׃
records.gloss: And said the watchman, I see the running of the first like [the] running of Ahimaaz son of Zadok. And said the king, A man good [is] this, and with news good he comes.
pieces: The watchman said, "It looks to me as if the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok." "He is a good man," the king said. "He is coming with good news."

L.27: And the watchman said, "I see the running of the first [is] like the running of Ahimaaz son of Zadok." And the king said, "This [is] a good man, and he comes with good news."

R.27: The watchman said, "I think the first man is Ahimaaz son of Zadok. I can tell by the way he runs." The king said, "He is a good man. He must be bringing good news."

decisions.choice: the running of Ahimaaz: he could be known by his stride
decisions.reason: A runner could be recognized from far away by the way he ran, as Jehu is recognized by the way he drives (2 Kings 9:20).

decisions.choice: a good man ... good news: the king hopes the messenger matches his news
decisions.reason: David reasons that a loyal man like Ahimaaz would be sent with good news. He is right about the victory but has not yet heard about Absalom.

decisions.choice: I think the first man is Ahimaaz ... I can tell by the way he runs.
decisions.reason: Readable states the watchman's guess first and then his reason.

records.source: וַיִּקְרָ֣א אֲחִימַ֗עַץ וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֶל־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ שָׁל֔וֹם וַיִּשְׁתַּ֧חוּ לַמֶּ֛לֶךְ לְאַפָּ֖יו אָ֑רְצָהסוַיֹּ֗אמֶר בָּרוּךְ֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ אֲשֶׁ֤ר סִגַּר֙ אֶת־הָ֣אֲנָשִׁ֔ים אֲשֶׁר־נָשְׂא֥וּ אֶת־יָדָ֖ם בַּֽאדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And called out Ahimaaz and said to the king, Peace! And he bowed down to the king [with] his face to the ground and said, Blessed [be] Yahweh your God, who has shut up the men who lifted their hand against my lord the king.
pieces: Ahimaaz called out to the king, "All is well!" He bowed down before the king with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed be {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hands against my lord the king!"

L.28: And Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, "Peace!" And he bowed down to the king with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed [be] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, who has delivered up the men who lifted their hand against my lord the king!"

R.28: Ahimaaz called out to the king, "All is well!" Then he bowed down low in front of the king with his face to the ground. He said, "Praise {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God! He has handed over to you the men who rebelled against my lord the king!"

decisions.choice: peace: all is well
decisions.reason: The word is a greeting and also a report: the battle has gone well for the king.

decisions.choice: delivered up: handed over the rebels
decisions.reason: The verb means "shut up", and so "hand over" an enemy into someone's power (1 Samuel 17:46; 24:19; 26:8).

decisions.choice: lifted their hand against: rebelled against
decisions.reason: To raise the hand against a king is to rebel (20:21; 1 Kings 11:26-27).

decisions.choice: Blessed be Yahweh your God: praise to God for the victory
decisions.reason: Ahimaaz gives the credit for the victory to Yahweh, not to Joab or the army.

decisions.choice: Praise the LORD your God! He has handed over to you
decisions.reason: Readable says "praise" for the old blessing formula, makes a new sentence of the clause about what Yahweh did, and says "rebelled" for the idiom.

decisions.choice: All is well!
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "Peace"; Balanced and Readable give its sense here.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ שָׁל֥וֹם לַנַּ֖עַר לְאַבְשָׁל֑וֹם וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲחִימַ֡עַץ רָאִיתִי֩ הֶהָמ֨וֹן הַגָּד֜וֹל לִ֠שְׁלֹחַ אֶת־עֶ֨בֶד הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ יוֹאָב֙ וְאֶת־עַבְדֶּ֔ךָ וְלֹ֥א יָדַ֖עְתִּי מָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said the king, [Is there] peace to the young man, to Absalom? And said Ahimaaz, I saw the great tumult at sending [the] servant of the king, Joab, and your servant, and not I know what.
pieces: The king asked, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz answered, "I saw a great commotion just as Joab was sending the king's servant and your servant, but I do not know what it was about."

L.29: And the king said, "[Is there] peace for the young man, for Absalom?" And Ahimaaz said, "I saw the great commotion when Joab sent the king's servant and your servant, but I do not know what [it was]."

R.29: The king asked, "Is young Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab was sending the king's servant and your servant, I saw a lot of noise and confusion. But I do not know what it was about."

decisions.choice: is there peace for the young man: is he safe?
decisions.reason: "Peace" here means safety and well-being. David's first question is not about the battle but about his son. The Cushite is asked the same question (verse 32).

decisions.choice: when Joab sent the king's servant and your servant: Joab sent the Cushite and Ahimaaz
alternatives: when the king's servant Joab sent your servant
decisions.reason: The Hebrew order is awkward: "at the sending of the king's servant, Joab, and your servant". It is best taken to mean that Joab sent two men: the king's servant, the Cushite, and Ahimaaz himself. It can also be read as "when the king's servant Joab sent your servant". Either way Joab is the one who sent them.

decisions.choice: I do not know what it was: Ahimaaz avoids the question
decisions.reason: Joab had told Ahimaaz that the king's son was dead (verse 20). Ahimaaz now says he does not know, perhaps to avoid giving the bad news himself.

decisions.choice: commotion: the noise and stir of a crowd
decisions.reason: The word means the roar and uproar of a crowd.

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: "Your servant" is the polite way to speak of oneself to a superior, as in Genesis 18:3 and 1 Samuel 20. It is kept at every level.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ סֹ֖ב הִתְיַצֵּ֣ב כֹּ֑ה וַיִּסֹּ֖ב וַֽיַּעֲמֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And said the king, Turn aside, stand here. And he turned aside and stood.
pieces: The king said, "Step aside and stand here." So he stepped aside and stood there.

L.30: And the king said, "Turn aside; stand here." And he turned aside and stood [still].

R.30: The king told him, "Move over and stand here." So he moved to one side and waited.

decisions.choice: turn aside, stand here: wait to one side
decisions.reason: The king does not accept Ahimaaz's vague answer and has him wait for the second runner.

decisions.choice: waited
decisions.reason: Readable says what standing aside meant.

records.source: וְהִנֵּ֥ה הַכּוּשִׁ֖י בָּ֑א וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַכּוּשִׁ֗י יִתְבַּשֵּׂר֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּֽי־שְׁפָטְךָ֤ יְהוָה֙ הַיּ֔וֹם מִיַּ֖ד כָּל־הַקָּמִ֥ים עָלֶֽיךָ׃ס
records.gloss: And look, the Cushite came; and said the Cushite, Let receive news my lord the king, for has judged you Yahweh this day from [the] hand of all those rising up against you.
pieces: Just then the Cushite arrived, and he said, "Good news for my lord the king! Today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has vindicated you by rescuing you from all who rose up against you."

L.31: And look, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Let my lord the king receive news, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has vindicated you this day from the hand of all who rose up against you."

R.31: Just then the Cushite arrived. He said, "My lord the king, here is good news! Today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has rescued you from all who turned against you and shown that you were in the right."

decisions.choice: let my lord the king receive news: a herald's opening
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of bringing good news (verse 19), here in the form "let him be told good news".

decisions.choice: judged you from the hand of: vindicated you by rescuing you
decisions.reason: As in verse 19.

decisions.choice: those who rose up against you: the rebels
decisions.reason: To "rise up against" someone is to attack or rebel against him.

decisions.choice: vindicated
decisions.reason: As in verse 19.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶל־הַכּוּשִׁ֔י הֲשָׁל֥וֹם לַנַּ֖עַר לְאַבְשָׁל֑וֹם וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַכּוּשִׁ֗י יִהְי֤וּ כַנַּ֨עַר֙ אֹֽיְבֵי֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְכֹ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־קָ֥מוּ עָלֶ֖יךָ לְרָעָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And said the king to the Cushite, [Is there] peace to the young man, to Absalom? And said the Cushite, Let be like the young man [the] enemies of my lord the king and all who rose up against you for harm.
pieces: The king asked the Cushite, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" The Cushite replied, "May all your enemies, my lord the king, and all who rise up to harm you, end up like that young man!"

L.32: And the king said to the Cushite, "[Is there] peace for the young man, for Absalom?" And the Cushite said, "May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you for harm, be like the young man!"

R.32: The king asked the Cushite, "Is young Absalom safe?" The Cushite answered, "I hope that everyone who is against you, my lord the king, and everyone who tries to hurt you, ends up the way that young man did!"

decisions.choice: may your enemies be like the young man: Absalom is dead
decisions.reason: The Cushite gives the news as a wish for the king's enemies. It is a respectful way of saying that Absalom is dead, but it still tells a father that his son was the enemy.

decisions.choice: verse numbers: the Hebrew text ends chapter 18 here
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. The next verse, where David weeps "my son Absalom", is 19:1 in the Hebrew text and 18:33 in many Bibles, and so the rest of chapter 19 is one number higher here than in those Bibles. The words are the same; only the numbers differ.

decisions.choice: I hope that everyone who is against you ... ends up the way that young man did
decisions.reason: Readable gives the wish as "I hope" and says "everyone who is against you" for "enemies".
